Stop spreading exaggeration and hyperbole.
There's a little brigade around here who hate Microsoft, apparently and reason doesn't seem to work on them.
Get this unsubstantiated FUD out of here.

I'm not impressed by the privacy things in windows 10 either but I have to say the fud machine seems to be at Vista level swing for Windows 10. I think this one might be dead in the water if history serves as an example. Vista wasn't 10% as bad as it was made out to be but it got sunk completely by exaggeration and misinformation.

And it also illustrates the problem with DRM only affecting people who want to play by the book. It's not going to affect people who circumvent DRM for means of piracy. In my mind DRM has always been more about controlling the experience of customers that play by the rules than preventing piracy. I think that forcing online requirements on single-player games is an extension of that.

So Windows is blocking old rootkits that were included with games; I'm okay with that. As far as I'm concerned this is on the publishers for shipping what amounts to malware with their games in the first place. It may even help build pressure for decrapified releases of old games.

Luckily PC gaming has gotten a lot better about this in recent times, and the few old ones that are affected are trivially cracked.

I guess my hangup is that I don't want Windows making that decision for me. Telling me what can run, what hardware is allowed, when updates are applied. Windows 10 takes a lot of control out of my hands, and with this issue specifically I'd rather have the option to run whatever programs I want without Windows stepping in on my behalf.

I don't disagree there. Something out of the way that regular users wouldn't find, like a registry setting, to allow this stuff would be a good thing. 99% of normal users wouldn't even know how to mess with it while allowing those that know what they're doing to make their own decision.

I think that's a very reasonable compromise. Most of my issues with Windows 10 are not necessarily it's default behaviors, but more the behaviors that can't be disabled, like the automatic updates. In this case having a registry option would be ideal because it preserves user choice while still strongly discouraging insecure behavior.
